articles.title: In 1952, a retired Canadian undertaker began saving empty embalming-fluid bottles: Around 500,000 bottles and 250 tons of glass later, he had built a castle-like home
articles.summary: Rest of World News: David H. Brown retired from the funeral business in 1952 after 35 years as an undertaker, when he began collecting empty bottles that had once held em.
articles.body: David H. Brown retired from the funeral business in 1952 after 35 years as an undertaker, when he began collecting empty bottles that had once held embalming fluid. Brown believed the square glass containers could have another use, and over time, that idea grew into a full-scale construction project on the shores of Kootenay Lake in British Columbia, Canada. The result was a two-story home built with around 500,000 discarded embalming-fluid bottles, with a castle-like front and a cloverleaf-shaped layout.The story of the house is documented by SPACES Archives, which records that Brown began the project in 1952. The archive describes the structure as having the footprint of a three-leaf clover, while crenellations across the front gave it an appearance more associated with a small castle than a conventional retirement home. The bottles had previously been used to hold formaldehyde embalming fluid in Brown's own profession and were collected from undertakers and funeral-industry colleagues.He collected bottles from funeral homes across western CanadaKootenay Rockies Tourism says that Brown traveled across western Canada to collect bottles from friends in the funeral profession, and eventually, he had acquired about 500,000 square-shaped embalming-fluid bottles. Together, the glass reportedly weighed around 250 tons. Brown's used the bottles as a building material, and Kootenay Rockies Tourism quotes him as saying the project began because he wanted to "indulge a whim of a peculiar nature." The same account says Brown had concluded that the discarded bottles should have some practical use after he retired.The containers were square, which allowed them to be arranged more easily than ordinary round bottles. SPACES Archives explains that they were laid horizontally, and their mouths and necks were pointed inward. Their square bottoms formed the outside surface of the house. Wood lath was wired between the bottle necks to hold the arrangement in place, while cedar planking formed the interior walls, and the building was therefore more than a collection of bottles embedded in concrete. Brown developed a structure around the glass and incorporated it into the walls themselves. Kootenay Rockies Tourism.The bottle collection became a 1,200-square-foot houseThe finished building measured roughly 48 feet long and 24 feet wide, with about 1,200 square feet of floor space. SPACES Archives records six round rooms, including a full kitchen, two bedrooms and a fireplace. It was two stories high, and the walls were made from hundreds of thousands of glass bottles, while the facade had crenellations resembling the upper edges of a castle wall. The surrounding property also became part of Brown's larger project. A wishing well, waterwheel, bridge, stone walls and other smaller structures were added to the grounds. Kootenay Rockies Tourism also describes a glass-bottle bridge and a path leading toward the lakeshore.Brown and his wife had originally intended to use the building as their private residence, and that changed as people traveling along Highway 3A near Boswell began stopping to see it. SPACES Archives says the Browns eventually decided to open the property to visitors rather than keep it solely as a home. It stands near Kootenay Lake, south of Boswell in southeastern British Columbia. The house remains one of the more unusual examples of reuse architecture in the region because of the scale of Brown's collection and the specific source of the containers.The house is still standing more than seven decades laterThe Glass House still exists at 11341 Highway 3A even seventy years after its construction began. SPACES Archives lists its status as "Extant," which means that the structure remains standing, while current regional tourism listings continue to advertise it as a visitor attraction. The Kootenay Lake Chamber of Commerce currently lists the Glass House as open for paid tours seven days a week from May through October. Its listing identifies the property as being made from more than half a million embalming-fluid bottles and provides the same Highway 3A location near Boswell.It began in 1952 as a retired undertaker's attempt to find another use for empty bottles and ended with a house made from about 250 tons of glass. The building was never hidden away as a private curiosity, and drivers still stop along the Kootenay Lake route to see the bottle walls, the cloverleaf-shaped structure and the former funeral-industry containers that Brown turned into a home.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Global ocean temperatures hit record high as El Nino intensifies
articles.summary: Copernicus warns of ‘unprecedented strain’ on world’s oceans as El Nino and climate change drive up sea temperatures.
articles.body:
The average global sea surface temperature has reached its highest level on record, a European Union agency said, warning that a rapidly intensifying El Nino and human-caused climate change were putting “unprecedented strain” on the world’s oceans.

In a statement on Monday, the EU’s Copernicus Climate Change Service said sea surface temperatures hit 21.1 degrees Celsius (69.98 degrees Fahrenheit) on Friday and Saturday, surpassing the previous record of 21.09C (69.96F) set in March 2024.

“This record is another clear signal of an ocean under growing stress,” said Samantha Burgess, the strategic lead for climate at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF). “El Nino is adding heat to the system, but it is doing so on top of decades of human-driven warming.”

Copernicus called the timing of the new record “particularly notable”. It said global ocean temperatures usually peak in March and April, when the summer in the Southern Hemisphere – which is mostly ocean – draws to a close.

But this year, the record was set in August.

Burgess told The Associated Press news agency that the oceans will keep getting hotter until the current El Nino – a natural temporary warming of parts of the Pacific that then warps weather and raises temperatures globally – reaches its peak, which is expected sometime between November and January.

The World Meteorological Organization, too, said it expects El Nino to strengthen in the coming months, and Copernicus said its seasonal forecasting system indicates that the event “could reach levels not seen for several decades”.

The added heat from El Nino comes as long-term fossil-fuel-driven warming has already raised ocean temperatures by 0.8C (1.44F), Burgess noted.

Copernicus also warned that rising ocean temperatures have “far-reaching consequences” for marine ecosystems and coastal communities.

Warmer oceans contribute to sea-level rise through thermal expansion, it said, and increase the likelihood and intensity of marine heatwaves, which can damage coral reefs and seagrass beds. This can in turn disrupt food chains and threaten industries such as fishing and aquaculture.

Warmer oceans are less able to absorb carbon dioxide, too, it said, weakening one of the planet’s key defences against climate change.

Higher ocean temperatures can also supply more heat and moisture to the atmosphere, enhancing the “potential for extreme weather events”.

Jane Lubchenco, an oceanographer and former head of the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, called the finding “very troubling”.

“An ocean this warm destabilises weather patterns and threatens food security, economic prosperity and marine life,” Lubchenco told the AP. “A warmer ocean is not our friend.”

articles.title: Rescuers find no trace of 22 missing crew days after cargo ship sinks in Bay of Bengal
articles.summary: Rescuers searching for 22 missing sailors have found no trace of their Panama-flagged cargo ship after the vessel sank in the Bay of Bengal last week, the In...
articles.body:
NEW DELHI (AP) — Rescuers searching for 22 missing sailors have found no trace of their Panama-flagged cargo ship after the vessel sank in the Bay of Bengal last week, the Indian Coast Guard said Tuesday.

Search aircraft and ships on Tuesday were scouring the area where the cargo ship MV Ocean Winner reportedly sunk Saturday about 276 miles (444 kilometers) from the Paradip coast of India's eastern Odisha state.

The joint search by the Indian Coast Guard and Indian Navy has been complicated by the area's exceptionally deep waters and found only an oil slick and two life rafts near the vessel's last known position, officials said.

The lack of wreckage has hampered efforts to determine the cause of the sinking and where to focus search operations, authorities said.

The vessel transporting iron ore to China was carrying 24 crew members, including 20 Chinese nationals, three Myanmar nationals and one Bangladeshi, according to the coast guard.

Two Chinese crew members were rescued Saturday following a distress call from the ship, the coast guard said.

articles.title: In 1999, the Azores protected forest for the endangered Azores bullfinch; two decades of restoration later, surveys estimated about 1,300 birds in suitable habitat
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover how dedicated conservation efforts have helped restore the Azores bullfinch population from 100 pairs in 1999 to over 1,300 individuals today by revitalizing their habitat in the Azores.
articles.body: In 1999, the Azores set aside the Pico da Vara/Ribeira do Guilherme region on SÃ£o Miguel Island for the conservation of the endangered Azores bullfinch, a bird found nowhere else in the world. At the time, the bird species had been reduced to around 100 breeding pairs and survived in a small remnant of native laurel forest. More than two decades later, sustained habitat restoration transformed about 1,000 acres of its core habitat, and surveys estimated the bird population at around 1,300 individuals. The Smithsonian notes that this recovery followed years of removing invasive plants, restoring native forests, and planting more than 500,000 native trees.A species confined to a shrinking forestThe Azores bullfinch, locally known as the Priolo and scientifically as Pyrrhula murina, is endemic to SÃ£o Miguel, the biggest island in the Azores archipelago, and its decline followed centuries of changes to the islandâs native vegetation. A 2011 study published in Bird Conservation International evaluated annual monitoring data from 1991 to 2008, confirming that the historical population decline had successfully halted and stabilised shortly after the 1999 conservation measures were enacted. Instead of a continuing downward spiral, this tracking window proved that protecting the remaining laurel forest on the eastern side of the island provided an immediate, vital lifeline against habitat degradation.The birdâs dependence on native vegetation made habitat restoration central to its survival. Jamie Ramosâ research, which was later published in Biological Conservation, helped establish the importance of the bullfinchâs diet and habitat preferences. The study showed that the species feeds on a range of native plants and their seeds, buds and other parts, meaning that replacing native forest with invasive vegetation could reduce both available habitat and food. Ramosâ work reportedly helped conservationists conclude that protecting and expanding native forest was more important than simply trying to manage the bird directly.Notably, the conservation situation was serious enough that the International Union for Conservation of Nature listed the Azores bullfinch as Critically Endangered in 2005. However, the formal protection of its core habitat had already begun by then, with the Pico da Vara/Ribeira do Guilherme area designated for bird conservation in 1999. This milestone established the legal framework necessary to secure international funding over the next four years.The process of removing invasive plants and rebuilding native forestFollowing the administrative steps, major restoration work began in 2003, when the Portuguese Society for the Study of Birds (SPEA), working with the Azores government and European Union LIFE funding, began a dedicated conservation programme. Smithsonian reported that the first five-year project concentrated on improving forest quality by planting native trees. Later LIFE projects expanded the work, including establishing a nursery capable of producing a large number of native plants.Conservationists had to remove the invasive vegetation that had displaced the native plants. Managed in sequence, the LIFE Priolo project ran from 2003 to 2008, followed immediately by the LIFE Sustainable Laurel Forest project from 2009 to 2013. These projects restored around 275 hectares of laurel forest, which is roughly 680 acres, while later projects continued the restoration in the protected area.This work restored around 1,000 acres of core laurel forest over approximately two decades, with more than 500,000 native trees planted. Specifically, the European Commissionâs LIFE program notes a broader project footprint of roughly 450 hectares (about 1,112 acres) actively managed. This restored core area ultimately acted as an ecological engine, improving environmental quality across the wider region.In 2010, the IUCN moved the species from Critically Endangered to Endangered when a comprehensive, modernised census estimated the population at 1,000 birds, and then to Vulnerable in 2016. These changes indicate that the Azores bullfinch had successfully moved away from its steep downward trajectory and achieved population stabilisation.By 2023, data published by the European Commission reported that the population had grown to around 1,300 individuals. Benefiting from the core restoration work, these birds successfully expanded out into nearly 5,000 acres of suitable regional habitat now available within the wider protected zone. While different wildlife survey methods can produce varying baseline numbers, such as a parallel annual report estimating 1,061 individuals, both data models confirm that the population has achieved long-term stability.Therefore, the recovery cannot be reduced to a single number or single intervention. Six LIFE projects have supported conservation work over decades, while invasive plants and introduced mammals remain threats. A bird once restricted to a shrinking fragment of native forest now occupies a substantially larger area with improved conservation status.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: Apple threw a farewell party for its outgoing chief at Apple Park on Sunday, spilling out of CaffÃ¨ Macs, the cafeteria tucked into the ring-shaped Cupertino headquarters, and into the courtyard at its centre, where OneRepublic performed in the round. A photo on X shows Cook holding a guitar, standing with the band.About 200 people were there, almost all of them Apple employees, The Information reported. Somewhere in the evening, Cook did something he has done publicly only once before in his 15 years running the company. Speaking to the room, he acknowledged his partner and called him by his first name, Mike.Laurene Powell Jobs and Jeff Williams were among those who paid tributePowell Jobs, wife of Apple co-founder Steve Jobs, spoke at the event. So did Jeff Williams, the chief operating officer who retired last year, and Eddy Cue, who runs services and health. John Ternus, the hardware engineering boss taking over as Apple CEO next Tuesday, also offered remarks. There were no politicians and no celebrity parade, just a room made up almost entirely of colleagues.Tim Cook has kept his personal life off the record since coming out in 2014He came out in a Bloomberg Businessweek essay in October 2014, writing that being gay had given him "the skin of a rhinoceros", which he said came in handy in his job. He described the decision as a trade-off with his own privacy and said he did not consider himself an activist. In the twelve years since, he has spoken far more often about privacy as a principle than about himself.John Ternus becomes Apple CEO on September 1 as Cook moves to executive chairmanApple announced the handover in April. Ternus joined the product design team in 2001 and has spent almost his entire career at the company. Cook becomes executive chairman, a role Apple says will include engaging with policymakers around the world, and Arthur Levinson shifts from chairman to lead independent director.The Information also reports a smaller detail that tells you what Apple is going for here. articles.title: Man dies in crash after Stratford-upon-Avon police pursuit
articles.summary: Two women are also hurt and one remains in hospital in critical condition.
articles.body:
A man has died and two women have been injured in a crash after a police pursuit near Stratford-upon-Avon.

Officers tried to stop a black Audi on Birmingham Road shortly before 17:30 BST on Monday but the driver failed to pull over, Warwickshire Police said.

A pursuit began and 15 minutes later the Audi crashed into a white Ford Puma, the force added, with the Audi's 19-year-old male driver confirmed dead at the scene by paramedics.

The driver of the Ford, a woman, was seriously injured and remains in hospital in critical condition, while injuries to a second woman - her passenger - were serious but not believed to be life-threatening. An investigation by the police watchdog is under way.

Officers said after failing to stop, the Audi made off in the direction of the A46 before travelling back towards Stratford on the A439 Warwick Road where the crash occurred.

A number of other cars were damaged during the pursuit, police said.

Warwick Road was closed on Monday from the Marraway roundabout to its junction with Ingon Lane and Sand Barn Lane, with the stretch remaining shut on Tuesday morning.

A spokesperson for West Midlands Ambulance Service said paramedics found four patients in total at the scene.

They included a man who was in a critical condition to whom crews gave advanced life support.

"Despite their best efforts, it became clear that nothing more could be done to save him and he was confirmed deceased by ambulance staff at the scene," the spokesperson said.

A woman who was driving the second car suffered life-threatening injuries, the ambulance service confirmed, and was taken to hospital in a critical condition. She was said by the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) to be in her 70s.

A female passenger in the vehicle was also seriously hurt and taken to hospital, although her condition was not thought by the ambulance service to be life-threatening.

Injuries to another patient from the car were not believed to be serious.

Supt Steve Flavell said: "Our thoughts are with the families of everyone involved in this collision... at this extremely difficult time.

"We made a mandatory referral to the IOPC because a death had occurred following police contact.

"They have declared an independent investigation and we will co-operate fully with their investigation."

The IOPC said the investigation was at an early stage and confirmed its officials attended the police's post-incident operation to gather information.

"We understand the driver of a black Audi A3 failed to stop for police and was then pursued for around six minutes before the vehicle was involved in a collision with a car being driven by a member of the public," a spokesperson said.

"We are also appealing for any car footage of the pursuit that other motorists may have recorded. Our investigators can be contacted at 0300 303 5609 or by email: WarwickRoadPursuit@policeconduct.gov.uk

"We have met with the families of the driver and the seriously injured woman to explain our role and will keep them regularly updated throughout our investigation, which is at an early stage."

Manuela Perteghella, Liberal Democrat MP for Stratford-on-Avon, said the incdent was "incredibly tragic".

"My thoughts are with the families of all those impacted. We must now let the investigation take its course."

Works were carried out on Warwick Road two years ago, aimed at reducing the number of crashes in the area.

Warwickshire County Council added a one-way system, lowered the speed limit and implemented a protected turning lane at the Ingon Lane junction.

Street lighting was also boosted to improve visibility for crossing pedestrians at Fisherman's Car Park.

"We understand the driver of a black Audi A3 failed to stop for police and was then pursued for around six minutes before the vehicle was involved in a collision with a car being driven by a member of the public," a spokesperson said.

"We are also appealing for any car footage of the pursuit that other motorists may have recorded. Our investigators can be contacted at 0300 303 5609 or by email: WarwickRoadPursuit@policeconduct.gov.uk

"We have met with the families of the driver and the seriously injured woman to explain our role and will keep them regularly updated throughout our investigation, which is at an early stage."

Manuela Perteghella, Liberal Democrat MP for Stratford-on-Avon, said the incdent was "incredibly tragic".

"My thoughts are with the families of all those impacted. We must now let the investigation take its course."

Works were carried out on Warwick Road two years ago, aimed at reducing the number of crashes in the area.

Warwickshire County Council added a one-way system, lowered the speed limit and implemented a protected turning lane at the Ingon Lane junction.

Street lighting was also boosted to improve visibility for crossing pedestrians at Fisherman's Car Park.

articles.title: In 2012, a 67-year-old Chinese duck farmer refused to leave his five-storey home; officials built a highway around it before paying him 260,000 yuan to move
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Explore the remarkable story of Luo Baogen, a 67-year-old duck farmer in China whose five-storey house resisted demolition as authorities built a highway around it, sparking international attention and discussions on property rights.
articles.body: In Wenling, an eastern Chinese city in Zhejiang Province, a five-story house once stood alone in the middle of a newly paved road, surrounded by a makeshift traffic circle. The house belonged to Luo Baogen, a 67-year-old duck farmer who had built it with his wife for more than 600,000 yuan around 2001. When local authorities cleared the neighborhood for a new access road, Luo and his wife resisted relocation for several years, even as workers built the road around their home.While 459 households accepted relocation, Luo did notIn 2008, the Wenling government planned to relocate about 459 households in Xiayangzhang to make way for a main road in front of the cityâs new railway station. The project required relocating 459 households in the village of Xiayangzhang, and by the time construction started, Luo and his wife were the only holdouts. The first offer was estimated at 220,000 yuan and then increased to 260,000 yuan. However, Luo contended that even the second offer was still far too low in comparison with what it would cost him to reconstruct another house, as he had already invested more than 600,000 yuan in building the previous one.Rather than wait for the dispute to end, workers paved a road around Luo's house, leaving the five-story building in the middle of a large roundabout. Photos of that scene started circulating online in late 2012 and made Luo's house one of the most recognizable Chinese "nail houses" (the term is used for buildings resisting demolition).Luo kept electricity, water and cable through the standoff Unlike many nail house holdouts, who are often cut off from basic utilities as pressure to leave mounts, Luo and his wife still had mains electricity, running water and cable television at the time of the report, based on the South China Morning Post. That made his case unusual among nail houses, where utilities are sometimes cut off to pressure occupants. As time went on, he continued to refuse the 260,000 yuan offer, saying it was far less than the 800,000 yuan he would need to build the same house elsewhere, while construction was completed and the road had not yet been opened to traffic.Luo accepted 260,000 yuan and a new plot of land Luo eventually signed a demolition agreement on November 30, 2012, after further talks with local officials and his family. Under the terms, the Wenling government paid him 260,000 yuan and provided a separate parcel of land for a new house, according to China's state Xinhua news agency, cited in a report from the Bangkok Post. âIt was never a final solution for us to live in a lone house in the middle of the road,â Luo Baogen told Xinhua. âAfter the governmentâs explanations, I finally decided to move.The excavators pulled down the house on the very next day, December 1, 2012, after pictures of the property garnered international media attention. According to Chen Xuecai, the head of Xiayangzhang village, Luo had grown tired of the attention, with reporters visiting the house daily during the final stage of the dispute. Luo's case became the most famous example of a dispute that has repeatedly occurred in China during large-scale development projects. Such disputes were common even in big cities like Chongqing, Shanghai and Guangzhou, where local governments or private companies sometimes built roads around a property whose owner refused to move.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Russian stadium says it won't host Kanye West gigs
articles.summary: Two planned concerts are thrown into doubt, but Russian promoters insist they will go ahead.
articles.body:
The Russian stadium that was scheduled to host two shows by Ye, the rapper also known as Kanye West, has said the events will no longer take place.

In a social media post , St Petersburg's Gazprom Arena said no rental agreement had been signed with the concert promoters. "Accordingly, the concert cannot take place on our site."

West would have been the first major Western performer to play Russia since it invaded Ukraine in 2022. The rapper is trying to rehabilitate his image after years of antisemitic remarks, for which he recently apologised.

Gazprom Arena acknowledged it had received complaints about West's planned appearance and stressed that it "was not and is not" responsible for his booking.

The stadium said in its statement that the sold-out concerts, scheduled for 10 and 11 October, had been organised by the Moscow-based Say Agency.

Posting on its Telegram channel, Say Agency said the stadium's announcement had come as a surprise.

"We learned about [it] at the same time as you did, through the media," the agency wrote. "As of now, the Ye concert has not been canceled," it added in a follow-up message.

"We are trying to contact the venue to find out the reason for the post and resolve the issue. We will keep you updated."

The BBC has contacted West's publicist for a comment on the uncertainty over his Russian shows.

In its statement, Say Agency said it announced the concerts earlier this month based "on an official letter that was approved by" Gazprom Arena.

The stadium subsequently sent a rental agreement, Say Agency claimed, and the agency acknowledged the contract had not yet been signed but said the deadline to do so did not expire until later this week.

Last week, Gazprom Arena had posted enthusiastically about the concerts on social media, calling Ye "the most influential musical artist of our time".

Fans reacted to its latest announcement with disappointment.

"This was the shortest concert of my life," responded one, under Say Agency's Telegram post. "It's a shame that the government is putting obstacles in your way," added another.

There is no indication that authorities intervened in the shows, but there has been opposition to West's booking from some Russian politicians.

Vitaly Milonov, a notorious conservative lawmaker, suggested the star should perform traditional Russian songs instead of his planned setlist, reflecting the anti-Western views of many nationalists.

"Maybe after this he'll stop his disgusting antics and become a normal person," Milonov added in a video statement.

West's antisemitic remarks began in 2022, when he made a series of offensive comments on social media that led to his accounts being suspended. Fashion brands like Adidas and Balenciaga also ended their relationships with the star.

The musician went on to declare he was "a Nazi", releasing a song called Heil Hitler and selling T-shirts featuring the swastika.

This January, West apologised in a full-page advertisement in the Wall Street Journal, writing: "I am not a Nazi or an antisemite."

Reflecting on a "four-month-long manic episode of psychotic, paranoid and impulsive behaviour", he said he was "deeply mortified" by his actions and that his bipolar disorder meant "you're manic [and] you don't think you're sick".

However, some questioned the timing of his statement - which coincided with the release of a new album, Bully, and the start of his world tour.

He held his first major concert in the United States in more than five years in Los Angeles in April, but planned shows in England, France, Italy and Poland have been cancelled over his past behaviour.

Say Agency acknowledged the controversy in a Telegram post last week , but defended its decision to bring West to Russia.

"Not everything Kanye West said should be forgotten," it said.

"Many people are talking about Kanye today. Many are trying to criticise him for words spoken during difficult times.

"But it's easy to judge based on a single statement. It's more difficult to listen to a person who has been changing the industry for decades. We listened, and we want to remind you."

articles.title: In 2017, Florida scientists tested mosquitoes around Burmese pythons; three mosquito species contained python DNA in their blood meals, suggesting insects could help locate hidden giant snakes
articles.summary: US News: Soon a mosquito may be assigned the job of hunting one of the Evergladesâ most elusive predators. For the uninitiated, Burmese pythons are one of the .
articles.body: Soon a mosquito may be assigned the job of hunting one of the Evergladesâ most elusive predators. For the uninitiated, Burmese pythons are one of the most concerning invasive species in South Florida, as they can hide in dense vegetation, wetlands, and remote areas, making them notoriously difficult to find. Now, researchers have examined a strange strategy: allowing mosquitoes to discover where the giant snakes may be lurking. In the journal PLOS ONE, a study by Lawrence E. Reeves called "Interactions between the invasive Burmese python, Python bivittatus Kuhl, and the local mosquito community in Florida, USA," appears to suggest something beyond imagination, where it is thought that mosquitoes might become python detectives. The idea was based on doctoral research by Lawrence Reeves, a post-doctoral researcher at the University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences Florida Medical Entomology Lab in Vero Beach. Reeves and his research team examined the interactions between Burmese pythons and mosquitoes, an ecological relationship that had been largely ignored. While the effects of pythons on the animals they eat are fairly obvious, we know much less about their interactions with animals that eat them or otherwise interact with them. The researchers collected mosquitoes from a Burmese python facility in Florida, where the snakes were housed in outdoor cages. And when they examined the blood within the mosquitoes, they found Burmese python DNA in the blood meals of three different species of mosquito. The discovery also opened up the unlikely possibility that mosquitoes could one day serve as biological trackers of hidden pythons. Scroll down for the details.How the technique would work"While a mosquito is feeding, it ingests blood from its host," the research paper reads. And if you can get the DNA from that blood meal, you might be able to tell what animal the insect was feeding on most recently. This means that mosquitoes caught in the wild could provide clues to the presence of Burmese pythons in an area. Rather than searching every marsh or clump of vegetation for a well-camouflaged snake, researchers could simply gather mosquitoes and test their blood meals for python DNA. This technique could be used to produce tiny biological surveillance devices from common insects.Why Burmese pythons are so hard to findBurmese pythons are a major detection challenge because they are extremely adept at avoiding humans, the study shows. Their coloration and semi-aquatic lifestyle provides them with camouflage and the ability to inhabit hard-to-reach wetlands and more remote habitats. They are large, and thus may seem easy to spot, but often the opposite is true. A python can hide itself in the vegetation or in places that are hard for people to reach.Researchers have tried various methods to locate the invasive snakes, including volunteers searching for pythons, specially trained detection dogs, and experienced snake hunters from Indiaâs Irula community. All methods have their limitations; manual searches can be time-consuming, and remote terrain makes access difficult. Mosquito-based detection could be another possible tool for identifying areas with pythons.From snake tracking to ecosystem surveysThe team believes the method can be used for more than just locating individual pythons. Testing mosquitoes for python DNA could help scientists track the invasive snakes and conduct biodiversity surveys. Mosquitoes can travel through areas that are hard for researchers to access directly, and they can potentially provide biological clues from places not easily reached by humans. The technique would not necessarily replace current methods of catching or removing pythons. Instead, it can help researchers narrow their search and identify places worth a closer look.Could mosquitoes spread diseases from pythons?This finding raises another important scientific question. Would mosquitoes that feed on Burmese pythons be able to pick up pathogens from the snakes and transmit them to other animals? Scientists have previously studied connections between mosquitoes, snakes and diseases. Other snakes are believed to be involved in transmission of viruses such as West Nile virus and Eastern equine encephalitis virus. Burmese pythons are also vulnerable to infection with some pathogens. Studies have found that snakes can become infected with the chikungunya virus and then infect mosquitoes, but the wider significance of this route is unknown. Thatâs why scientists want to know if mosquitoes feeding on Burmese pythons could help spread disease in the ecosystem of the Everglades.A little bug with a major potential roleThe finding illustrates how research on invasive species can go off in unexpected directions. A mosquito may be a tiny irritant compared to a giant python, but the blood it drinks can contain valuable genetic information about the animals itâs encountered. If researchers can make this approach work in the wild, mosquito surveillance could be another weapon in the fight to track Burmese pythons across South Florida. Right now the research is an interesting possibility: Instead of asking humans, dogs, or trained snake hunters to find the hidden pythons, scientists may be able to ask the mosquitoes where they have been.Images Courtesy: istockCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: US removes Syria from terrorism list after 46 years - what it means for the Middle East country
articles.summary: US News: The United States on Monday removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism, ending a designation that had been in place since 1979 and imp.
articles.body: The United States on Monday removed Syria from its list of state sponsors of terrorism, ending a designation that had been in place since 1979 and imposing significant restrictions on trade, investment and financial transactions with the country.The move, which followed a 45-day congressional review, marks a further step in Washingtonâs efforts to deepen ties with Syriaâs new government under President Ahmed al-Sharaa. The US also revoked the designation of the Nusrah Front, later known as Hayâat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), as a Specially Designated Global Terrorist organisation. The Treasury Department announced corresponding sanctions relief.âThese actions were all taken in recognition of the positive actions taken and further commitments by the Syrian government under President Ahmed al-Sharaa to fully distance Syria from acts of international terrorism,â US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement.Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the measures would encourage investment and support Syriaâs economic recovery. âToday's action will help foster additional investment in Syria to promote political and economic stability,â he said.The Treasury said the changes were âin line with President (Donald) Trump's promise to deliver sanctions relief to Syriaâ. It added that the removal of the restrictions âdoes not change Treasury's posture with regards to countering global terrorism and our commitment to hold bad actors in Syria accountable.âThe state sponsor designation had remained a major obstacle for businesses and financial institutions considering investment in Syria, even after the US ended its broader sanctions programme against the country in July 2025. The designation restricted US foreign assistance, defence exports and sales, certain dual-use goods and financial transactions.The Treasury has since said US financial institutions can provide services to Syria, process payments involving Syrian banks and establish correspondent banking relationships, provided sanctioned entities are not involved.Syriaâs government welcomed Mondayâs decision, describing it as an opportunity to reconnect with the global financial system and attract investment needed for reconstruction after nearly 14 years of war.Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shibani had earlier called the terrorism designation the âlast obstacleâ to rebuilding economic ties. âThere is no longer any obstacle to investment, doing business and rebuilding economic life in Syria,â he said.The US designation had been imposed in 1979, when Washington accused the government of then-President Hafez al-Assad of supporting militant groups. It continued under his son Bashar al-Assad, who was overthrown by rebels led by Sharaa in December 2024.HTS, formerly known as the Nusrah Front, was once affiliated with al Qaeda in Syria before breaking ties with the group in 2016. Sharaa later led the rebel coalition that toppled Assad and became president.With Syriaâs removal, Cuba, Iran and North Korea remain the three countries on the US state sponsors of terrorism list.The latest decision follows a broader rapprochement between Washington and Damascus. US President Donald Trump has backed sanctions relief for Syria and met Sharaa during a visit to Turkey, as the new Syrian government seeks international support for economic reconstruction.Syrian officials have also been pursuing closer links with international financial institutions and companies. The country's finance ministry has held discussions with Bank of America executives, while Mastercard has announced work with QNB Group and Syriaâs central bank to develop infrastructure for international card payments.Washington has said its engagement with Damascus is aimed at supporting Syriaâs stabilisation, economic recovery and reintegration into the global economy, while maintaining targeted measures against terrorism and other sanctioned actors.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: British man charged in Singapore two years after alleged theft at Changi airport
articles.summary: The 26-year-old faces up to seven years in jail for allegedly stealing a denim jacket from an airport shop in 2024.
articles.body:
Singapore has charged a British man for theft more than two years after he allegedly stole a denim jacket from a store at the airport shopping mall.

The police were alerted to the theft in the evening of 14 August 2024 when a retail assistant at Singapore's Changi Airport realised a blue denim jacket was missing from a display mannequin.

Surveillance footage showed a man removing the jacket, worth about S$350 ($275; £202), from the mannequin and leaving the store without making payment. By the time the authorities established his identity, the man had departed Singapore.

The 26-year-old was arrested on 15 August this year while in transit at the airport and was charged on Tuesday.

"The police take a serious stance of shop theft and will deal firmly with offenders in accordance with the law.

"Offenders should not assume that they can evade detection simply by leaving Singapore after committing an offence," the Singapore Police Force said in a statement on Monday.

In its statement the police also recounted a separate arrest of a 50-year-old Polish woman who had stolen two bottles of perfume from retail stores inside one of the airport's terminals on 11 June this year.

She was arrested in the transit area shortly before she was scheduled to depart Singapore. The woman was charged with two counts of theft on Tuesday.

Those convicted of theft in Singapore face up to seven years in jail.

articles.title: Deportees who refused to exit a U.S. flight in Liberia are sent to Equatorial Guinea
articles.summary: The six people from Cuba, Brazil and Cameroon were flown to another African nation as part of a third-country deportation deal with the Trump administration.
articles.body: DAKAR, Senegal — Six people who were deported by the United States to Liberia last week resisted getting off the plane and instead were sent to Equatorial Guinea, another African nation that signed a third-country deportation agreement with the Trump administration, a person on the plane and a lawyer in contact with the six said Monday. Under a series of often secret agreements, the Trump administration has deported thousands of people to two dozen countries that aren’t their own as it pushes ahead with its immigration crackdown, advocates say. Immigration lawyers say the practice is being used as a legal loophole to indirectly return some asylum seekers to countries they fled. The people who refused to get off the plane in Liberia on Thursday were four Cuban men, a Brazilian man and a Cameroonian woman, the person and the lawyer said. A Honduran deportee aboard the flight said the group refused to disembark, saying Liberia was “not their country” and that they would face danger there. They were then separated from the others, he said. He spoke on condition of anonymity out of fear of reprisals. He said the other passengers got off in Liberia because they feared officers would force them. Meredyth Yoon, litigation director for Asian Americans Advancing Justice-Atlanta, said the deportees who resisted leaving the plane in Liberia were told they would be returned to the United States but instead were flown to Malabo city in Equatorial Guinea. “It was a really heartbreaking and chaotic scene when they arrived in Malabo on Thursday,” Yoon said. Some arrived in chains and in extreme distress, she said, including the Cameroonian woman and one of the Cuban men, who Yoon said has a large abdominal growth and uses a colostomy bag that must be drained regularly. There is no medical staff at the hotel in Equatorial Guinea where the six are being held, alongside around 40 other deported migrants, she added. Conditions at the hotel have worsened in recent months, Yoon said, with food sometimes withheld and guards accused of threatening, beating and choking some of the migrants. Equatorial Guinea’s government did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Under an opaque $7.5 million deal with the Trump administration, Equatorial Guinea’s all-powerful president, Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo, has turned the hotel owned by his family into a prison for asylum seekers deported from the U.S. One of the Cubans sent to Equatorial Guinea was Carlos Rodríguez López, 35, who had been living in Miami Gardens, Florida. Igrayne Ribot, his wife and the mother of their daughter, said in an interview with the Telemundo affiliate in Miami that news of her husband’s deportation “arrived all of a sudden.” After receiving a notification about her husband’s transfer, she was able to reach him via video call. He told her he was in Africa. “I broke down,” she said. “Nobody imagines something like that — it was terrifying.”

articles.title: In 2009, Iceland drillers hit 1,000Â°C magma by accident, unlocking a geothermal source that could produce nearly 10 times more power
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In 2009, a drilling operation in northeast Iceland unexpectedly punched into molten rock at Krafla, revealing one of the hottest geothermal resources .
articles.body: In 2009, a drilling operation in northeast Iceland unexpectedly punched into molten rock at Krafla, revealing one of the hottest geothermal resources ever reached by a borehole. The Iceland Deep Drilling Project(IDDP) had been searching for high-temperature geothermal energy, but instead of finding only hot water and rock, the drill encountered magma at about 2.1 kilometres below the surface. Temperatures there were estimated at roughly 900â1,000Â°C. What followed turned an accident into an extraordinary energy experiment. Engineers managed to complete the well and draw superheated steam from the area around the magma, showing that heat close to molten rock could deliver far more energy than geothermal wells. The result also gave scientists a unique glimpse into a part of Earth that is almost impossible to reach, setting the stage for a more ambitious attempt to study and use magma.1000Â°C magma encounter become an energy experimentInstead of simply abandoning the well, the project team decided to find out what the unexpected magma encounter could actually do. The engineers installed a steel casing in the well, with the lower section perforated near the magma. The hole was then allowed to heat gradually. Eventually, it began producing extremely hot, high-pressure steam. IDDP-1 produced superheated steam for roughly two years, until July 2012. During testing, the steam reached temperatures above 450Â°C, making the well the hottest geothermal production well in the world at the time. The steam could also be fed directly into the existing Krafla power plant. The result was much more significant than setting a temperature record. It demonstrated that a geothermal well could operate extremely close to molten rock and draw useful energy from the intense heat surrounding it.What was the drilling team looking for in IcelandThe team was searching for a better source of geothermal energy. The IDDP was established to investigate whether extremely hot underground conditions could provide much more energy than conventional geothermal systems. At Krafla, in northeast Iceland, the project planned to drill far deeper than the point where most geothermal wells normally operate. According to PhysOrg, IDDP-1 was intended to explore high-temperature resources, with the original drilling programme taking the well towards depths of around 4.5 kilometres. Instead, the drill encountered something completely unexpected at just 2.1 kilometres which was molten rock with temperatures of approximately 900â1,000Â°C. The discovery was extraordinary because drilling directly into magma is extremely rare. Therefore, Krafla became a natural laboratory where scientists could study what happens when a well reaches the boundary between solid rock and molten material.Why was the well so much more powerfulThe reason was the enormous amount of heat available at such extreme temperatures. Conventional geothermal wells generally rely on naturally heated underground water. Superhot geothermal systems aim to reach much hotter conditions, where water carries substantially more energy. The âClean Air Task Forceâ reported that IDDP-1 could have generated up to 36 megawatts of electricity, equivalent to roughly 5-10 times the output of a typical commercial geothermal well operating at lower temperatures. It also described the well as the world's hottest production well when it reached 450Â°C during operation. The reason is relatively simple that when âwater is subjected to extreme underground heat, it can become superheated steam capable of carrying far more energy to the surface.â That is why the accidental discovery became so important. The drill had not simply found hot rock; it had revealed a potentially much more energy-dense geothermal resource.Challenges created by the extreme heat inside the wellThe same conditions that made IDDP-1 powerful also made it incredibly difficult to operate. The âClean Air Task Forceâ noted that the project faced severe corrosion while the well was heating up. The casing also had to withstand exceptionally hostile temperatures and fluids. Once the fluid became sufficiently hot, however, corrosion decreased substantially. The experience showed engineers that future wells would need carefully designed casings, valves, cement and surface equipment capable of surviving these conditions.The project also faced mechanical setbacks. According to AAPG, the drill became stuck and the team had to sidetrack the well during the effort. The experience nevertheless produced valuable information about drilling through extremely hot and pressurised underground environments. Eventually, IDDP-1 was shut down in 2012 after problems with surface equipment. But the experiment had already proved its central point that extremely hot geothermal resources could potentially produce dramatically more electricity from a single well.Foundation of the Krafla Magma Testbed(KMT)The unexpected discovery did not end with the IDDP-1 experiment. Instead, it inspired a much larger scientific ambition. The Krafla Magma Testbed (KMT) was developed as an international project designed to create the world's first magma observatory. Its aim is to deliberately access magma at Krafla and study it directly rather than waiting for another accidental encounter. KMT says the site is particularly valuable because a known magma body exists at relatively shallow depth, making Krafla an exceptional place for controlled research.The âInternational Continental Scientific Drilling Programâ states that rhyolitic magma at Krafla is known to exist at roughly 2.1â2.5 kilometres depth and around 900Â°C. Researchers hope to examine the boundary between the magma and surrounding rock, while also keeping the well available for long-term observations. The planned work is about more than electricity. Scientists want to understand how heat and fluids move around magma, improve instruments that can survive extreme underground conditions and learn more about volcanic systems.Could magma become a new source of geothermal powerThe Krafla experience suggests that it could, although major engineering challenges remain. KMT describes superhot geothermal resources as having the potential to greatly increase energy output per well. The project is being developed as both a research facility and a testbed for technologies that could eventually make these resources easier and safer to utilise. The AGU report also noted that KMT could help researchers understand how heat moves from magma into the surrounding geothermal system. One earlier analysis suggested that long-term flows of superheated steam from the IDDP-1 area could potentially produce more than 30 megawatts of electricity from a single well. The accidental drilling of 2009 ultimately changed the direction of geothermal research. Today, the goal is no longer to avoid magma. Scientists and engineers are increasingly asking whether, with the right technology, they can safely reach it, understand it and perhaps one day turn its extraordinary heat into a dependable source of clean electricity.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: BPSC exam row, 'dogs bark' remark: What has triggered fresh student protests in Bihar
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Chaotic scenes unfolded in Biharâs Patna on Tuesday as protesting students clashed with police during a massive protest over alleged irregu.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Chaotic scenes unfolded in Biharâs Patna on Tuesday as protesting students clashed with police during a massive protest over alleged irregularities in the 70th BPSC examination.The protest was met with a heavy police deployment, with barricades erected to stop the students from marching.Police also used water cannons as protesters attempted to push past the barricades.Later, the Samrat Choudhary-led government claimed it had addressed âalmost all issuesâ raised by the students. The protesters, however, said several long-standing demands remained unresolved and continued their agitation.The students marched from Gandhi Maidan towards Raj Bhavan.The protesting students also broke the barricades in bid to gherao chief minister's residence.The protest has also brought into focus delays in recruitment examinations, the proposed format of the Teacher Recruitment Examination-4 (TRE-4), alleged paper leaks and demands for greater transparency in Bihar's recruitment system.Govt says students' issues have been addressedBihar education minister Mithilesh Tiwari said the government had resolved the issues raised by the students and maintained that its doors remained open for further dialogue."All the issues over which the students were staging a sit-in have been resolved. It is not as if the student agitation was the sole reason for this; it is the government's very intent to resolve the problems faced by our youth in a timely manner. We have addressed every issue raised by the youth. I was surprised to hear a person who has never even taken a board exam offering suggestions on examinations. That is why I would say to Tejashwi Yadav to enroll in a Bihar government school, pass the tenth-grade exam, and then come back to offer us suggestions on examinations," Tiwari said.The minister said that almost all the demands had been met and invited students to approach the government with any remaining concerns."We have met almost all the students' demands. For any students who wish to convey further points to the government, the doors for dialogue remain wide open. Let the students come, talk, and get their issues resolved; the government belongs to them," he said.However, the protesters said their concerns had not been fully addressed and that problems related to the education system, examination paper leaks and delayed recruitment continued.'Do you need 1,800 years?' Students question recruitment delaysProtester Vikas Bhatt said the students were demanding improvements in Bihar's education system and action against repeated examination paper leaks."Our demand is that the education system in Bihar be improved. We are raising issues regarding the frequent exam paper leaks in the state. Look at the recruitment for librarians, it hasn't happened for 18 years; do you need 1,800 years? Whenever we stage a protest, they simply offer assurances and leave it at that. How can things go on like this? Three recruitment drives were announced through the BSSC, but it has been three years. We have repeatedly besieged the BSSC commission, demanding that the exam dates be announced. Despite this, they keep asking for 15 days' time. Apart from the BPSC, there isn't a single commission in Bihar that issues an annual calendar," Bhatt said.The students are demanding the cancellation of the 70th BPSC examination over allegations of irregularities and paper leaks.The agitation has also centred on the proposed TRE-4 examination. Students have opposed the proposal to conduct the examination in two phases across Bihar and are demanding that it be held in a single phase.They have also sought the immediate release of the official TRE-4 advertisement.Students break through barricades during Raj Bhavan marchAs the protest continued, students marched from Gandhi Maidan towards Raj Bhavan. Some protesters broke through police barricades and attempted to move towards the restricted area.Police used water cannons to disperse the crowd, while several protesters were detained.DSP Kamakhya Narayan Singh said the police would not allow the protesters to enter the restricted area, although he expressed hope that the ongoing talks between students and senior officials would lead to a resolution."We will stop them; we won't let them proceed further. However, the dialogue has been positive, and we hope the students will agree. They have raised several issues with the senior officials, and the outcome has been positive. So, I expect the turnout to be lower and that they will agree. If they don't, we will stop them right here. We won't allow them to enter the restricted area," Singh said.Congress leader Sushil Kumar, who was present at the protest site, said the government had failed to give assurances on several key demands."We want to state clearly that a single-stage examination must be implemented for TRE 4.0 at all costs, and negative marking should be abolished. There are numerous other issues as well, regarding the BPSC, BSSC, Sub-Inspector recruitment. The government has offered no assurances on any of these points. We have urged the Chief Minister to hold a dialogue; he should invite our delegation for talks. We have been on a hunger strike for nine days, yet no one is willing to listen to us. Just imagine, had the government engaged in dialogue, this situation would not have arisen. We are heading towards the Chief Minister's residence; the Chief Minister should hold talks, and our delegation will go there for the discussion," Kumar told news agency ANI.JD(U) says govt is serious about students' concernsJD(U) leader Shravan Kumar said the Bihar government was taking the concerns of students and job seekers seriously and was acting according to established rules and legal provisions."The government is taking the demands and concerns of students and job seekers seriously. Everything is being done for them in accordance with established rules, laws, and provisions. Bihar is the first state in the country to have made such large-scale recruitments across government departments," Kumar said.He also pointed to the government's employment target for the 2025-2030 period and urged young people not to be influenced by the opposition."It is Nitish Kumar's resolve to provide 10 million (1 crore) jobs and employment opportunities to the people of Bihar between 2025 and 2030. Recruitments are taking place in every sector, and vacancies are being announced in every department. I urge our youth to exercise patience and not fall for the opposition's ploys; they are not going to provide jobs. They merely intend to exploit your hard work and sweat to further their own political interests. Beware of them," he added.Tejashwi writes to Samrat ChoudharyMeanwhile, Bihar leader of opposition Tejashwi Yadav has written to chief minister Samrat Choudhary over the ongoing BPSC row, urging the government not to ignore the students' demands and to hold talks for an early resolution.Tejashwi has demanded that TRE-4 be conducted as a single examination across the state. He has also sought an end to what he described as discrimination against Hindi-speaking candidates in the BPSC Civil Services Main Examination and interview.The RJD leader has further demanded complete transparency in all competitive examinations, including those for Sub-Inspector, Constable, BSSC and BPSC recruitments.Among his other demands are a high-level independent inquiry into alleged irregularities in past examinations, strict action against recruitment mafias and time-bound schedules for all pending tests.He has specifically called for clear timelines for the BSSC Intermediate, CGL, ASO, BSO, Librarian and Accountant recruitment examinations.RJD scion Tejashwi remark also followed BPSC official's "dog-barking" remark. Bihar LoP also called for action for his remark referring to students.Bihar launches monthly student support campsAmid the continuing protests, the Bihar government on Tuesday launched the monthly 'Vidyarthi Sahyog Shivir' or student support camps to address students' grievances.The camps will be organised at educational institutions on the fourth Tuesday of every month, chief minister Samrat Choudhary said in a social media post."The Bihar government is launching Vidyarthi Sahyog Shivir starting today to ensure prompt resolution of students' grievances. These camps will be organised at educational institutions on the fourth Tuesday of every month," Choudhary wrote.The camps will allow students to raise their grievances directly with the concerned government officials. Students will also be able to register complaints online and track their status through the portal and Helpline 1100.The government's announcement comes as the student protest continues in Patna's Gardanibagh area, with the two sides offering sharply different views on whether the protesters' demands have been addressed.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Family of Alex Pretti speaks out in exclusive interview: 'They murdered our child'
articles.summary: Pretti was shot and killed by federal officers on Jan. 24.
articles.body:
Seven months after 37-year-old Alex Pretti was shot and killed by two federal immigration officers in Minneapolis, his grieving family said they want "accountability" in their first television interview.

"We've seen what happened. The videos are pretty clear. But we want justice. We want accountability for the people that did this to Alex," his father, Michael Pretti, said in the exclusive interview with "Good Morning America" co-anchor George Stephanopoulos while joined by his wife and daughter.

Alex Pretti , an American citizen and ICU nurse for the Department of Veterans Affairs, was killed on Jan. 24, roughly two weeks after fellow U.S. citizen Renee Good was shot and killed by an ICE officer in Minneapolis during the Trump administration's "Operation Metro Surge" immigration crackdown. Both shootings sparked nationwide outrage and demands for accountability over federal officers' deadly use of force in Minneapolis.

Michael Pretti said his son was observing immigration activity when the shooting occurred.

"He cared deeply about his community. Minneapolis was his community. He wanted people to be treated fairly, no matter what walk of life, what their background was," Michael Pretti said.

Watch the interview with the Prettis and George Stephanopoulos on "Good Morning America," airing Tuesday, Aug. 25, at 7 a.m.

Eyewitness video shows that Alex Pretti appeared to be recording when a federal officer shoves a woman into him. He seems to try to help her, and then both of his hands are visible -- one holding a phone and the other held up, seemingly to protect himself from pepper spray -- when he's wrestled to the ground. His firearm, which he had a legal permit to carry, was removed by an officer while he was on the ground and before approximately 10 shots were fired, the video shows.

A minute-by-minute timeline of the fatal shooting of Alex Pretti involving federal agents

His parents said they found out their son had been shot while watching the coverage of the shooting on the news. His mother said she recognized her son's jacket and sunglasses from the footage.

"That's how we found out, watching it on TV. Watching our son be shot ten times on TV," Michael Pretti said.

"In the back," Susan Pretti, Alex's mother, added.

"I was not shocked that he helped somebody. My shock is that he was murdered and no one has given us the complete truth or anyone has been held accountable. And it's been seven months," Susan Pretti said.

"What did he do to deserve to be murdered? To be left cold, on the ground, dead, my child? What did he do?" she asked.

In the wake of the deadly shooting, some Trump administration officials were quick to blame Alex Pretti. Former Border Patrol Commander Greg Bovino said it looked like Pretti wanted "to do maximum damage and massacre law enforcement," and then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem claimed he "committed an act of domestic terrorism."

Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller posted on social media that he was an "assassin" and "domestic terrorist."

When asked about the response, Michael Pretti said, "There was more effort in vilifying him than pursuing justice, investigating this."

After video of him in a confrontation with federal agents 11 days before the shooting surfaced on social media, President Donald Trump called Alex Pretti an "agitator" and "perhaps" an "insurrectionist" in a social media post.

Asked what it felt like to hear those things said about their family member, his sister, Micayla Pretti, said, "I don't think you would like my answer."

"It's so un-presidential," Michael Pretti said. "It's ridiculous that, you know, the leader of the free world speaks that way about an American citizen."

Susan Pretti said she wants an apology for what was said about her son. "Why shouldn't we get one?" she asked.

The Department of Justice opened a federal civil rights investigation into the shooting. Steve Schleicher, an attorney for the Pretti family, told ABC News that they don't know where that stands or what information they've gathered.

"They at least have the right to know who shot Alex Pretti," Schleicher said. "They have the right to be consulted with meaningfully, they have the right to meet with the prosecutors, they have the right to have the process not drag on too long. They have the right to be informed, and that's just not being done here."

In a letter to then-Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche last month, Schleicher said that the U.S. attorney in Minnesota met with the Pretti family on July 13 but that "the meeting raised more questions than answers."

2nd Amendment backlash follows portrayal of Alex Pretti by some Trump administration officials

A DOJ spokesperson said in a statement to ABC News, "As is standard protocol, family member communications, if any, come at a later stage of a case, such as at indictment, initial appearance, plea, trial, or sentencing. Communications with family do not typically occur during an investigation."

The Department of Homeland Security and FBI are also involved in the investigation, the DOJ said. A DHS spokesperson told ABC News that the investigation remains active, while the FBI declined to comment.

ABC News asked the White House if Trump and Stephen Miller still stand by what they said about Alex Pretti, but they did not answer the question.

A DHS spokesperson said the agency "works to give the American people accurate information as quickly as possible. These statements were made based on information received on the ground from CBP."

"This is a law enforcement matter and an active investigation and we refer you to FBI for further questions. We urge individuals not to impede any law enforcement action and ICE operations," the spokesperson said.

Asked what justice looks like for them, Micayla Pretti said she wants the names of the agents who shot her brother officially released.

"They murdered our child," Susan Pretti said. "People need to be held responsible when they murder people in this country. Period."

articles.title: Rajnath Singh approves transfer of DRDO missile technology to Indian defence industry
articles.summary: News News: NEW DELHI: Defence minister Rajnath Singh has approved the transfer of DRDO-developed technologies for all conventional missile systems to Indian defe.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Defence minister Rajnath Singh has approved the transfer of DRDO-developed technologies for all conventional missile systems to Indian defence companies for production within the country, the defence ministry said on Tuesday.The move is aimed at accelerating indigenous missile manufacturing, reducing import dependence and expanding the role of domestic companies in India's defence ecosystem.The ministry described the technology transfer as an "important milestone" in increasing industry participation and enabling the transition of missile systems from development to industrial production."The provision will enable successful transition of missile system development to industrial production, reflecting the continued efforts of DRDO (Defence Research and Development Organisation) to leverage the capabilities of the Indian industry for the development and manufacture of advanced defence systems," the ministry said.Under the initiative, Indian defence companies will be able to undertake production of DRDO-developed conventional missile technologies, subject to applicable qualifications, certifications and regulatory requirements.The government said the move is intended to strengthen India's domestic defence industrial base and expand manufacturing capabilities.The initiative will also create opportunities for Indian micro, small and medium enterprises and other technology partners to participate in missile production and related supply chains.The defence ministry said the initiative would increase domestic value addition while supporting the growth of India's defence manufacturing sector.DRDO will continue to work with Indian industry to facilitate the transfer and absorption of advanced defence technologies, the ministry said.

articles.title: Who are Iran’s top trading partners US would need to target to isolate it?
articles.summary: The US wants to isolate Iran from the global economy. Here is who Tehran trades with, and how much is at stake.
articles.body:
United States Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has unveiled a new wave of sanctions on Iran, branded “Operation Economic Outcast”, designating close to 60 entities, individuals and vessels and widening secondary sanctions to cover shipping, gold, aviation, technology and digital assets.

He said the aim was to sever every economic lifeline sustaining the government in Tehran until it stands alone, and that President Donald Trump was telephoning world leaders with specific requests to halt their dealings with Iran, though he named no countries and set no deadline.

Below, we break down Iran’s top trading partners using official customs figures compiled by Trade Data Monitor, which exclude the unrecorded flows sustaining much of Iran’s oil exports.

Iran has spent much of the past two decades under Western sanctions, a pressure that has pushed its economy away from Europe and towards a narrowing group of Asian and regional partners.

In 2024, Iran exported some $56bn worth of goods to at least 112 countries and territories, according to official customs figures. Its top export partners were:

China ($14.58bn) – The largest buyer of Iranian oil, taking more than 80 percent of Iran’s seaborne crude exports, according to tanker-tracking analysts. Much of it is discounted and moved by shadow-fleet vessels, barely registering in either country’s customs records.

Iraq ($11.7bn) – Iran has been a major supplier of gas to Iraq for electricity generation, and sells electricity directly to Iraqi provinces in the south. It is also a leading source of food products, building materials and manufactured goods.

UAE ($7.16bn) – Has long been a financial and re-export lifeline for Iran, accounting for 13 percent of its exports. Abu Dhabi imposed an indefinite trade embargo last week after accusing Iran of firing missiles at its territory. Tehran denied the allegations.

Turkiye ($6.1bn) – Iran has long supplied Turkiye with pipeline gas via the Tabriz-Ankara Pipeline, along with petrochemicals, food products, and construction materials.

Afghanistan ($2.3bn) Iran supplies its landlocked neighbour with fuel, food and construction materials, and Afghanistan depends heavily on Iranian ports and overland routes to access wider markets.

In 2024, Iran imported some $68.5bn worth of goods from at least 87 countries and territories, according to official customs figures. Its top import partners were:

UAE ($21bn) – Supplied just above 30 percent of Iran’s imports, most of them re-exported goods rather than Emirati production, giving Tehran indirect access to Western machinery, electronics and consumer goods. Abu Dhabi’s indefinite trade embargo has severed that route.

China ($17.8bn) – The main supplier of machinery, electronics, vehicles and industrial components, and the partner Iran has leaned on most heavily as Western trade has closed off.

Turkiye ($11.1bn) – A shared land border and longstanding commercial ties make Turkiye a key overland supply route, sending machinery, chemicals, vehicles and manufactured goods. Trade in both directions has fallen since the war began.

European Union ($6.1bn) – European sales are now a fraction of pre-2018 levels, concentrated in pharmaceuticals, medical equipment and machinery.

India ($1.6bn) – Trade has fallen sharply in recent years. New Delhi has kept commercial links narrow and weighted towards agricultural goods including rice, tea and pharmaceuticals.

articles.title: Tottenham Hotspur complete the signing of Savinho
articles.summary: Tottenham Hotspur have completed the signing of Manchester City winger Savinho in a reported £85 million deal.Spurs are said to be paying an initial £75 mill...
articles.body:
Tottenham Hotspur have completed the signing of Manchester City winger Savinho in a reported £85 million deal.

Spurs are said to be paying an initial £75 million for the 22-year-old with a further £10 million to potentially be paid in add-ons.

"It's taken a while but I'm very happy to be here," the Brazilian said on his arrival.

"It's a wonderful opportunity at a brilliant club with one of the best managers in the world.

"As soon as I spoke to the Head Coach I knew I had to come. He told me he wants to help me reach the highest level, and I believe we can do that together, as a team."

Savinho first joined City in a controversial transfer from fellow City Football Ground club Troyes , after having never featured for the French side.

In total, Savinho featured 84 times for City during his time at the club, scoring seven times and making 13 assists.

articles.title: U.S. cancels South Korea marine drills over tied up forces in Iran war
articles.summary: The United States cancelled a joint amphibious landing drill scheduled for next month with South Korea, Seoul’s Marine Corps said on Monday, after Washington cited constraints on the availability of U.S. forces due to the war in Iran.
articles.body: SEOUL, South Korea — The United States canceled a joint amphibious landing drill scheduled for next month with South Korea, Seoul’s Marine Corps said Monday, after Washington cited constraints on the availability of U.S. forces due to the war in Iran. The U.S. Marine Corps formally notified its South Korean counterpart in June that force availability would be constrained for the division-level exercise, known as Ssangyong, a South Korean Marine Corps spokesperson told a news briefing. The allies remain in close consultations on resuming the drills, the spokesperson said. He did not specify what measures might be taken to prevent future cancellations or to make up for lost training opportunities. U.S. Forces Korea did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Later on Monday, the U.S. State Department said that Secretary of State Marco Rubio had spoken with South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun about a “range of issues” in their alliance. Rubio told his South Korean counterpart that Washington and Seoul need to remain in close coordination on matters integral to their alliance, according to a State Department statement. The cancellation of the amphibious landing drill follows President Donald Trump’s surprise order to scale back a separate annual joint military exercise that ended last Friday, citing the cost and Seoul’s refusal to take part in the Iran war. North Korea — whose leader, Kim Jong Un, Trump has repeatedly expressed interest in meeting again — has long condemned such joint exercises as rehearsals for invasion. Referring to North Korea, Trump also wrote on his Truth Social platform that the Ulchi Freedom Shield drills sent “a signal that was totally inappropriate and hostile, to a Country that, as long as Donald J. Trump has been President, has been unthreatening and respectful.” Despite the reduction of the exercises, Pyongyang fired 10 short-range ballistic missiles last week and issued a statement denouncing the exercises.

articles.title: Kremlin adviser warns UK drone factories could face attacks
articles.summary: Russia says UK decision to share missile blueprints with Ukraine is evidence of direct military involvement in the war.
articles.body:
Factories manufacturing drones in the United Kingdom for export to Ukraine could come under attack from “unknown sources”, a Kremlin adviser has said, after Britain agreed to share long-range missile blueprints with Kyiv.

Andrei Fedorov, an adviser to the Kremlin and a former deputy foreign minister, told British broadcaster BBC on Tuesday that he could not “exclude 100 percent” that there might be some “semi-military” action against Britain, as UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham visited Ukraine.

The UK shared missile blueprints with Ukraine for it to manufacture French-British designed long-missile drones during Burnham’s first overseas trip to Kyiv on Monday. Sharing these blueprints, according to the Russian adviser, is seen by Moscow as proof of the UK’s “direct military involvement” in the Russia-Ukraine war.

Fedorov said that “sooner or later, there might be not only verbal but maybe some visible reaction from Russia towards the UK”.

Asked to elaborate, he said: “There are different discussions how it should look like – it might be so-called technical reaction, maybe some hackers attack from unknown source, not from official level, of course.”

“There might be different political steps, and I cannot exclude 100 percent that there might be some semi-military.”

“For example, something might happen with enterprises, with the factories which are producing drones for Ukraine, etc.”

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov shared similar sentiments with reporters on Monday, stating that the UK is “participating in this war” by its missile support and that this is adding “fuel to the fire”.

Burnham responded in Kyiv by asking reporters who started the fire in the first place. Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

The UK has agreed to declassify blueprints for British-made components for the Scalp missile, a French-produced version of the Storm Shadow that has already been used to hit targets in Russia.

The Scalp missile can hit targets that are heavily fortified, such as bunkers, unlike existing Ukrainian missiles. It has a range of about 240km (149 miles).

Ukraine has increased its production of cheaper drones significantly in the past year, attacking more economic and military targets within Russia.
