articles.title: In 1997, a horse jumped a fence and joined one of Franceâs prestigious cycling races; it ran through the peloton and reached the front before leaving 20 kilometres from the finish
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In March 1997, amidst the professional cyclists of the CritÃ©rium International, a horse jumped onto the course, raced with the peloton, and became an unforgettable and chaotic part of the race's history.
articles.body: In March 1997, the CritÃ©rium International peloton suddenly gained an unexpected companion: a horse. The animal had jumped a fence beside the course and landed directly in the path of the fast-moving cyclists. Rather than turning away, it ran alongside the riders, moved through the group and eventually reached the front. The interruption became one of the most memorable moments in the history of the race.According to Cyclingnews, the incident took place on March 29, 1997, during the opening stage of the CritÃ©rium International, a French stage race held in the Tarn region that year. The 188-kilometre stage ran from Blaye-les-Mines to Rabastens and featured riders such as Laurent Jalabert, Marco Pantani and Chris Boardman. Late in the race, a horse escaped from a field and joined the peloton, creating confusion among the riders. The animal remained with the group for several kilometres before falling away and disappearing from the race, with reports placing the incident roughly 15 to 20 kilometres from the finish.When the peloton met a runaway horseThe riders were travelling together when the horse suddenly cleared a fence bordering the road. Television footage captured the animal landing on the course and immediately joining the stream of cyclists. For the riders, the appearance was more than a curiosity; it was a serious hazard. A horse running at speed in the middle of a tightly packed peloton could easily have caused a serious crash. FrÃ©dÃ©ric Moncassin later recalled the dramatic sound of the animal landing, describing the noise of its hooves, the sparks and its breathing. The horse, however, did not panic. It continued forward with the cyclists.Rather than remaining behind the pack, the animal began moving through it. It passed riders and worked its way towards the front, creating an extraordinary scene in which a four-legged intruder appeared to be competing against some of Europe's best professional cyclists. The horse eventually reached the front of the group and crossed the bridge at Lisle-sur-Tarn ahead of the riders. When the cyclists approached a junction, the race turned while the horse continued straight ahead, finally leaving the course and ending its unexpected appearance in the race.The race continued without its unexpected challengerThe horse may have been the most memorable part of the opening stage, but the race continued and produced a very different story over the following two stages. In the first stage, StÃ©phane Barthe of Casino won the 188-kilometre route from Blaye-les-Mines to Rabastens in a sprint, finishing ahead of Mario Traversoni and FrÃ©dÃ©ric Moncassin. His victory gave him the early overall lead, while the horse that had briefly joined the peloton became an unusual footnote to the day's racing.The Cyclenews also notes that the following morning overall standings changed during the mountain stage to Pic de Nore. He went on to win the 1997 CritÃ©rium International overall, leaving the horse as the unlikely star of the race's opening day.From cycling footage to film historyWhat began as a bizarre moment during a professional cycling race did not remain confined to the world of sport. Footage of the horse running alongside the peloton was later used in AmÃ©lie, the 2001 French film directed by Jean-Pierre Jeunet, giving the incident a second life on screen. The horse had appeared during the opening stage of the 1997 CritÃ©rium International, a long-running French stage race that attracted many of the sport's leading riders and was often part of their preparation for bigger races later in the season.What made the footage so striking was not simply that a horse had wandered onto the course. articles.title: In the early 2000s, Mark Magura bought a 272-acre Indiana farm;  after a 3-year restoration, 200.6 acres came back as wetland, prairie and forest for wildlife
articles.summary: US News: Discover how Mark Magura transformed his 272-acre Indiana farm into a thriving wildlife habitat, restoring wetlands, prairie, and forest. Learn about the permanent conservation easement ensuring protection for future generations.
articles.body: For more than a decade, much of Mark Maguraâs Indiana property was simply farmland, with about 220 acres leased to farmers growing crops. Today, the landscape includes wetlands, prairie, young forest and shallow seasonal ponds that provide wildlife habitat. The transformation took three years and ultimately put 200.6 acres under a permanent conservation easement, ensuring that the restored land will not return to conventional farming.According to the US Department of Agricultureâs Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS), Mark Magura bought the 272-acre property in Starke County, Indiana, in the early 2000s. For more than a decade, about 220 acres remained in agricultural production under lease agreements with different farmers. During this period, Magura began working with the NRCS to enrol parts of the property in conservation programmes aimed at addressing wet areas and improving wildlife habitat.From farmland to wildlife habitatThe first steps came well before the major restoration. In 2006, Magura enrolled portions of the farm in the Conservation Reserve Program to address wet areas around drainage ditches. NRCS provided technical assistance, while the Farm Service Agency helped fund the planting of cool-season grass filter strips. Further changes followed in 2009 and 2010. Hardwood trees were planted to provide habitat for the Indiana bat, while warm-season grasses were established along field borders to benefit quail and other upland birds. As wildlife began returning, Magura became increasingly interested in restoring a much larger portion of the property.NRCS notes that Magura began the process of enrolling about 200 acres in the Wetland Reserve Easement programme in 2018. The restoration took three years and converted former cropland into a mix of wetland, prairie and forest habitat. Once the work was completed, the easement covered 200.6 acres and placed the land under permanent conservation protection. Under its terms, the property could not be returned to conventional agriculture or subjected to major landscape-altering activities such as drainage or timbering. Magura retained ownership of the land, but accepted permanent restrictions on how it could be used. He could still enjoy the property for activities such as hiking, fishing and hunting, and he could sell it if he chose, but the conservation easement would remain attached to the property and bind future owners as well. In this way, the agreement protected the restored habitat beyond Magura's own ownership, ensuring that the land's conservation purpose would continue even if its ownership changed.Building wetlands from a former farmOne of the most ambitious parts of the project was the creation of 16 acres of macrotopography, a network of shallow, pond-like depressions across the restored landscape. The depressions were built with different depths and shapes so they could collect and retain water at different times of the year, creating varied wetland conditions across the site.Research published in Wetlands Ecology and Management found that restoring seasonal flooding can help revive seasonal patterns in waterbird communities and increase bird diversity. The researchers found that restored flooded meadows supported greater waterbird diversity, with the effects particularly evident during autumn and winter. The findings highlight the ecological value of wetlands that experience changing water levels rather than remaining permanently flooded.The restoration involved more than creating shallow depressions. Trees were planted throughout the property, while prairie areas were established with conservation cover. Together, these efforts created a mosaic of wetland, grassland and forest habitats, with transitional areas between them. Instead of providing wildlife with a single type of landscape, the restoration created a more varied environment with different habitats in proximity.When wildlife returnedFor Magura, the clearest sign that the restoration was working came from the sheer amount of wildlife. The property that had once been dominated by corn and soybean fields was soon home to birds, frogs and other animals. At one point, the wildlife was so abundant that the sounds around his home disrupted the quiet he had expected to enjoy. The transformation also changed the long-term future of the property. Instead of treating the land solely as an agricultural asset, Magura chose to make much of it a permanent wildlife habitat.The result is a reminder that restoring farmland does not necessarily mean returning it to a single, fixed type of landscape. On the property, wetlands, prairie and forest now coexist, each providing different conditions for wildlife. The work took years, but once the major construction was completed, nature took over much of the next stage. As Magura put it, the land was something people could steward rather than own forever. His three-year restoration was only the beginning. The trees will continue to grow, the prairie will develop, and the seasonal wetlands will keep changing with the water table, allowing the landscape to become increasingly self-sustaining over time.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Perfectly fine with my body’: Danish PM blasts plastic surgeon’s beauty advice
articles.summary: Mette Frederiksen, Denmark’s second female prime minister, is one of Europe’s longest-serving and most experienced leaders.
articles.body: COPENHAGEN, Denmark — Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen is fed up with getting unsolicited beauty advice. The 48-year-old wrote Monday on Instagram that she had just returned home from a trip to Ukraine, where she was exposed to air raid sirens in the ongoing war, only to find a message by a plastic surgeon offering to “fix that little spot on your nose.” “I’ve lost count of how many messages I’ve received over the years about my appearance,” Frederiksen wrote. “Especially that I have ugly teeth and thin hair. That I have an ugly ‘wart’ on my nose and well-meaning advice to get some Botox.” The prime minister of the Nordic country posted a screenshot of the plastic surgeon’s offer on Instagram but without identifying him. She also posted her response: “Oh no. I’m happy with my body — I really don’t need a male plastic surgeon to have an opinion about it!” Frederiksen, a Social Democrat and Denmark’s second female prime minister, is now in her third term, making her one of Europe’s longest-serving and most experienced leaders. She has led the European Union and NATO member country since mid-2019. She has pledged to maintain a firm stance against U.S. President Donald Trump’s ambitions for Greenland, the kingdom’s semiautonomous territory, and continue supporting Ukraine against Russia’s war of aggression. On Instagram, Frederiksen stressed that she does not interfere with other people’s looks and that “I’m perfectly fine with my body — as it is when you’re a woman approaching 50.” She added that “if you’re going to write to me (and you’re more than welcome to), I hope you’ll use your time to talk about something more meaningful. Not my nose.” The prime minister also said that those unsolicited beauty tips and suggestions made her feel “indignant” and that “today, I’m sending an extra loving thought to all of you who have to put up with the ‘perfect imperfections’ we all walk around with every day.”

articles.title: In 1959, Vermont bought Snake Mountain land but the seller kept timber rights; 67 years later the state plans to secure 949 acres of those rights and add 256 acres
articles.summary: US News: A conservation story that began nearly seven decades ago is entering a new chapter in Vermont. What was once a complicated split between land ownershi.
articles.body: A conservation story that began nearly seven decades ago is entering a new chapter in Vermont. What was once a complicated split between land ownership and timber rights at Snake Mountain is now set to be reunited, potentially giving wildlife, forests and outdoor enthusiasts greater protection for generations to come. According to media reports, with support from the Trust for Public Land, the Vermont Fish & Wildlife Department plans to secure the timber rights covering 949 acres of the Snake Mountain Wildlife Management Area (WMA). The state also plans to acquire an additional 256 acres in Addison and Weybridge, expanding the popular natural area by nearly 25%. It is reported that both transactions are expected to be completed by early 2027.A major expansion for Snake MountainLocated between Addison and Weybridge, Snake Mountain WMA currently encompasses 1,215 acres of forested landscape surrounded largely by farmland. Its proximity to some of Vermontâs largest population centres makes it an especially valuable place for people seeking access to nature. The planned 256-acre addition would expand the protected area while improving habitat connectivity. The project is also expected to create new opportunities for hiking, hunting and wildlife watching. The effort will simultaneously reunite the stateâs ownership of the land with the timber rights covering much of the WMA, allowing Vermont Fish & Wildlife to take a more coordinated approach to managing the landscape.Why timber rights matterWhen Vermont purchased the lands that became Snake Mountain WMA in 1959, the seller retained the timber rights. This meant that while the state owned the land for conservation and public access, responsibility for growing, managing and harvesting timber remained with the private owner. Such arrangements have historically been relatively common on Vermont Fish & Wildlife properties. More than six decades later, the state is seeking to bring those interests together. Acquiring the timber rights would allow Vermont Fish & Wildlife to coordinate forestry decisions with its broader goals for wildlife, recreation, water quality and habitat protection. Any future roads or skid trails required for timber harvesting could also be planned alongside conservation priorities.A haven for wildlifeSnake Mountain is far more than a scenic hiking destination. The WMA contains eight types of wetlands, including a glacial bog estimated to be about 9,500 years old. Its forests and wetlands provide habitat for a remarkable range of species. Peregrine falcons nest on the mountainâs western cliffs, while mature trees provide roosting habitat for federally endangered Indiana bats and northern long-eared bats. The landscape also supports woodland mammals, game birds, songbirds, amphibians and other wildlife. Protecting and connecting these habitats could become increasingly important as environmental conditions change.Building climate resilienceConservation groups say the expanded and reunified property could play an important role in climate resilience. The larger protected landscape would provide additional lowland forest habitat while helping safeguard wetlands and headwater streams. These interconnected natural areas can serve as important refuges for biodiversity and help species adapt as the climate changes. For a forested landscape surrounded by farmland, strengthening those connections could be particularly valuable.How the project is being fundedThe timber rights and additional acreage are being purchased from The A. Johnson Co., LLC, with funding assembled from local, state, federal and private sources. The project includes a $1.35 million grant from the US Fish & Wildlife Serviceâs Recovery Land Acquisition Grant programme, funded through the Land and Water Conservation Fund. It also includes $417,500 from the Vermont Housing & Conservation Board, support from the Town of Weybridge Conservation Fund and significant private donations. The availability of federal funding is linked largely to the habitat provided by Snake Mountain for endangered bat species.A long history of conservationThe A. Johnson Co. has managed the timber rights at Snake Mountain for decades. The company has maintained that responsible forestry can coexist with wildlife habitat, recreation and healthy natural communities. The planned transfer marks an opportunity to bring those long-standing conservation and forestry interests under unified management. Vermont Fish & Wildlife officials say the agency is particularly appreciative of the stewardship that helped maintain the quality of the landscape over the past several decades.More land could soon join the WMASnake Mountainâs expansion may not end with the 256-acre acquisition. In 2026, the WMA is also expected to receive a donation from The Nature Conservancy consisting of two adjoining parcels totalling 88 acres in Addison. Known as the Willmarth Woods Natural Area, the property contains one of the Champlain Valleyâs largest low-elevation mature forest stands. The area features rich soils supporting a high-quality mesic red oak and northern hardwood forest. It also contains the trailhead for one of the main hiking routes leading to Snake Mountainâs summit. Planned as an addition to Snake Mountain WMA since 1992, Willmarth Woods could further strengthen the ecological and recreational value of the protected landscape.Image Courtesy: istockCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Overnight raid near Haiti capital kills around 50 - here is what happened
articles.summary: Rest of World News: At least 47 people were killed and another 22 injured in an overnight attack by armed gangs in Kenscoff, a hillside community overlooking Haiti's capi.
articles.body: At least 47 people were killed and another 22 injured in an overnight attack by armed gangs in Kenscoff, a hillside community overlooking Haiti's capital, Port-au-Prince. The UN estimated that casualty figures could potentially riseKenscoff, which overlooks key routes into the capital, has faced about a dozen attacks by armed gangs since last year, forcing thousands of residents to leave their homes.The gangs, operating under a broad alliance, have strengthened their control over Port-au-Prince for years and expanded into surrounding areas despite efforts by foreign countries to support Haiti's outgunned police.Haitian rights group RNDDH estimated that between 30 and 40 people were killed and 15 to 20 wounded in the latest raid. It said the attack began at around 10:30 p.m. local time and that the full death toll remained difficult to establish.The Haitian government condemned the incident as a "heinous attack" and pledged to strengthen security. However, residents called for the local police chief to resign, accusing officers of failing to protect people who were killed only minutes away from the police station."Kenscoff will not be abandoned," the Prime Minister's office said on social media, adding that government authority would be restored "without weakness and without delay."Residents forced to flee KenscoffUN estimates show that attacks in Kenscoff over two months in early 2025 killed more than 260 people and resulted in the destruction or burning of 200 homes. Around 3,000 people were forced to flee.Nearly a dozen further attacks have occurred since then, involving rape, kidnapping, arson and livestock theft.Residents said several dozen police officers attempted to repel the armed attackers during the night, with some officers reportedly injured. They also said they had not identified any gang members among those killed, Reuters reported.Local media reported that several houses were set ablaze, including the home of Jean William Pape, a prominent public health expert.Kenscoff overlooks routes leading to Petion-Ville, where several embassies, upscale hotels and the temporary seat of government are located. It also overlooks a major road connecting the capital with southern Haiti.According to Reuters, the latest violence could further raise concerns about Haiti's ability to hold an election in December, which would be the country's first in a decade. Successive governments have repeatedly postponed elections as armed gangs have expanded their influence.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

How much interest can I earn with a high-yield savings account?

The amount of interest you can earn from a savings account depends on the annual percentage rate (APY). This is a measure of your total earnings after one year when considering the base interest rate and how often interest compounds (savings account interest typically compounds daily).

Say you put $1,000 in a savings account at the average interest rate of 0.38% with daily compounding. At the end of one year, your balance would grow to $1,003.81 — your initial $1,000 deposit, plus just $3.81 in interest.

Now, let's say you choose a high-yield savings account that offers 4% APY instead. In this case, your balance would grow to $1,040.81 over the same period, which includes $40.81 in interest.

The more you deposit in an HYSA, the more you stand to earn. If we took our same example of a high-yield savings account at 4% APY, but deposited $10,000, your total balance after one year would be $10,408.08, meaning you'd earn $408.08 in interest. ​​

Deposit account rates — including savings rates — are tied to the federal funds rate . This is the target interest rate set by the Federal Reserve; when it increases its target rate, deposit account rates usually increase. Conversely, when the Fed lowers its rate, deposit rates fall.

Savings account interest rates have fluctuated quite a bit over the past couple of decades. From 2010 to about 2015, rates were rock-bottom, hovering between 0.06% and 0.10%. This was largely due to the 2008 financial crisis​ and the Federal Reserve 's decision to lower its target rate to near zero in order to spur economic growth.

From 2015 to 2018, interest rates gradually increased. However, they remained low by historical standards. Then, the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 led to another sharp decrease in rates as the Fed cut rates again to stimulate the economy. This brought average savings interest rates down to new lows, around 0.05% to 0.06%, by mid-2021.

Since then, savings account rates have recovered considerably, largely driven by the Fed's interest rate hikes in response to skyrocketing inflation. However, the Fed finally lowered the federal funds rate toward the end of 2024 and continued to do so throughout 2025. As a result, deposit rates have steadily declined. So far in 2026, the Fed has kept rates unchanged

Is now a good time to put your money in a high-yield savings account?

Choosing where to put your money is an important decision, and there are a few factors you should consider when evaluating your options. A high-yield savings account could make sense if you're looking for a secure place to hold shorter-term savings while earning a solid return.

Interest rates: One of the most important features of a savings account is the interest rate. It's important to shop around and compare the best offers to ensure your money will grow over time. Considering that savings rates will likely drop in the near future, opening a high-yield savings account now will allow you to take advantage of historically high rates.

Goals: Today's high-yield savings accounts offer rates we haven't seen in more than a decade. That said, savings rates still don't match average returns for the stock market. If you're saving for a long-term goal like retirement, a savings account probably isn't the best place to put your money, since your balance won't grow at a pace that will allow you to reach your target. However, if you're saving for a financial emergency, a down payment on a home or car, holiday gifts, or another short-term goal, a savings account is a great place to hold those funds.

Accessibility: Certain types of accounts and investments may provide higher returns than a savings account, but may make it difficult to access your funds in a pinch. For example, if you put your savings in a certificate of deposit (CD) and need to access the money before the maturity date, you could be subject to an early withdrawal penalty. So, if you want to be able to dip into your savings as needed, a high-yield savings account is likely the better choice.

Security: In most cases, savings accounts are insured by the FDIC up to the federal limit. They also can't lose money due to fluctuations in the market, making them a low-risk option.

Do online banks have the best savings account rates?

Online banks operate exclusively via the web. This significantly reduces their overhead costs, so they're able to pass those savings onto customers in the form of high deposit rates and low fees. In fact, many of the best high-yield savings accounts also come with zero monthly fees or minimum opening deposit requirements. If you're searching for the best savings interest rates, online banks are a great place to start .

That said, online banks aren't the only place you can find savings accounts with rates that range between 3% and 4% APY. Credit unions are not-for-profit financial cooperatives known for offering competitive rates and fewer fees. Many credit unions have requirements that must be met to become a member, though some allow just about anyone to join.

How to open a high-yield savings account

The requirements involved in opening a savings account vary by financial institution. However, if you're ready to open an account, you can follow these general steps:

Research savings account rates: Of course, when choosing a savings account, one of the most important factors to evaluate is the interest rate. Be sure that you select a savings account with a competitive rate to help your money grow.

Figure out your must-haves: Although savings account interest rates should be top of mind, that's not the only factor to consider. You'll also want to think about what else you need from your account, whether it's no minimum-balance requirement , low fees, or other perks. Finding a savings account with a solid rate that also helps you achieve your goals is key.

Prepare documentation: Opening a bank account requires you to provide a few important personal details and documents. Before you start your application, be sure you have your Social Security number, driver's license or passport number, and proof of address.

Fill out the application: In many cases, you can apply for a savings account online. However, some financial institutions may require you to visit the branch in person to apply. Either way, the application for a new savings account should only take a few minutes to complete. In many cases, you'll get your approval decision instantly.

Fund your account: Once your savings account application is approved, you'll need to add funds to the account. Be sure you're aware of any minimum opening deposit requirements and the timeline for funding.

Is a high-yield savings account right for you?

A high-yield savings account is a good fit if you want to earn a competitive return on money you'll need in the near future while keeping it safe and accessible. It's important to not only consider whether the interest rate is attractive, but whether the account matches the purpose of your savings.

You want to maximize your emergency fund.

You have extra cash sitting in a low-interest checking or traditional savings account.

You don't need to write checks or use the money for everyday spending.

An HYSA may not be the best choice if...

You're investing for retirement or another goal that's 10+ years away. Investing in a diversified portfolio has historically produced higher long-term returns, though with greater risk.

You won't need the money for a fixed period. If you can leave your savings untouched for several months or years, a certificate of deposit (CD) may offer a higher guaranteed yield.

You need frequent access to your money. A checking account is more convenient for paying bills and making everyday purchases.
